newsitem.title: USA: Chocolate cake firm seeks slice of world market.
newsitem.headline: Chocolate cake firm seeks slice of world market.

text.p: David Glass, creator of a critically acclaimed line of gourmet chocolate cakes, is eagerly serving up slices of his company to investors.
Desserts by David Glass Inc. is trying to raise $2 million in a stock offering, in hopes of becoming the nation's leading producer of gourmet cakes -- and one with global reach.
"We want to expand the product line and promote like crazy," Glass, the company's founder and president, said in an interview.
"The more mouths that we can put samples into, the more customers we'll have," Glass said. "Once people taste our cakes, they're hooked. It's like drugs."

Some 14 years after the company's founding, Glass's flagship product is still The Ultimate Chocolate Truffle Cake. The New York Times has said it is "considered by many chocolate lovers to be the ultimate dessert."
In his company's early days, Glass's tireless dishing out of free samples helped get his products into two New York City food meccas: Zabar's and Balducci's.
Today, Desserts by Glass has $1.1 million a year in sales, 14 employees, and national distribution through its annually published catalogue.
About 60 percent of the company's sales are in the Northeast. Glass products are also distributed in Canada and Italy.

Glass, 48, cites the marketing efforts of super-premium ice cream maker Haagen-Dazs as a worthy role model. His stock offering circular points out that the pricing of Haagen-Dazs products is not too high to preclude substantial sales.

The lanky, casually dressed Glass knows he's up against some formidable players in the prepared foods industry. But he thinks his company has built a loyal following since it grew out of his and wife Virginia's home catering business.
"There's not a lot of gourmet stuff out there," Glass said, seated in his factory-style office in Hartford's historic Colt Firearms Building.
"I worked in France at the best restaurants, and I'll only make something that I consider to be exquisite and unique."

A native of West Hartford, Conn., Glass worked in several Michelin three-star restaurants, including Archestrate (now Lucas-Carton) in Paris, Troisgros in Roanne, France, and Girardet in Crissier, Switzerland.
"During my time in these formidable kitchens, I decided that I would make some food product in the U.S. that was as good as or better than what these restaurants made," he said.
Glass insists on all-natural ingredients in his products, and even blends his own chocolate because he can't find the exact mix he wants on the market.
Most of the company's eight-inch cakes sold in catalogues weigh about 2 pounds, and retail for $25 to $30. Its six-inch cakes sold in retail outlets are priced at $7 to $10.
Glass has several expansion ideas in the oven, including increased distribution to major international airlines. His cakes are now on Northwest Airlines and Air Canada flights.
Glass is also pursuing big U.S. restaurant chain accounts. His cakes have featured in Planet Hollywood special events.

Other plans include selling single cake slices in "beautifully designed packages," Glass said. The company is receiving free advice on this project from Vermont ice cream maker Ben & Jerry's Homemade Inc., Glass said.

Glass is also developing chocolate cake shells, to be filled with mousse and liqueur-flavored whipped creams. Late last year, it introduced its latest product, The Ultimate Sophia Loren Luscious Italian Almond Cake.
Desserts by Glass sells to both retail and food service accounts. Its products are also sold in other companies' catalogues, including Starbucks Corp and Balducci's.

The stock offering, for up to 650,000 shares of common stock at $3 per share, is being marketed via the Internet. It is limited to residents of Connecticut, Massachusetts, New York, New Jersey, California, Washington, Florida, and the District of Columbia.
The shares will not be traded on a stock exchange. Instead, Glass's plan is to expand, reinvest net profits, and fatten up the company's attractiveness to prospective buyers.
